metadata.title: Examination of Turkish Middle School STEM Teachers' Knowledge about Computational Thinking and Views

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary data via an online questionnaire administered to 121 STEM teachers from 38 middle schools in Turkey; it does not describe the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is based on descriptive survey scales and group comparisons (MANOVA) and correlations (Pearson r), the manuscript does not report any student/sampling weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife). No PV-based scaling is involved because the dependent variables are questionnaire scale scores and a translated QCT test score rather than ILSA achievement plausible values. The analytic sample appears to be the full set of respondents who completed the questionnaire items required for the reported scale analyses; the paper notes that two QCT items were removed for analysis and three additional questions were not used, indicating instrument-level preprocessing rather than survey-weight preprocessing.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not analyze cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs) from an ILSA assessment; instead, it uses questionnaire Likert-type scales and a computational thinking conceptual development test score (QCT) administered to teachers. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not report a specific missing-data strategy for questionnaire items or QCT responses, so the missing-data handling approach cannot be verified from the text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used an online questionnaire completed by STEM teachers from 38 middle schools (34 public, 4 private) in seven cities in Turkey. The QCT instrument was translated into Turkish; two QCT items were removed because they did not work well for analysis, and three other questions were not used in the online questionnaire because they did not fit the research scope. Teachers were required to respond to each question on the online survey to gather adequate information for the study aims; the paper does not specify additional exclusion rules beyond the QCT item removals.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: QCT computational thinking conceptual development score
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA between-subjects effects: Graduation Wilks’ lambda k=0.115, F=9.19, p=0.009; but Table 5 shows QCT: Graduation F=0.115, p=0.742, eta^2=0.11. Experience QCT: F=1.013, p=0.459, eta^2=0.336. Discipline QCT: F=2.592, p=0.124, eta^2=0.341. Attending ICT–CT education QCT: F=0.342, p=0.796, eta^2=0.093. Mean QCT: M=8.80, SD=2.9 (17 items).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged educational discipline, teaching experience, graduation level, attending ICT–CT training, and ICT level in schools to analyze QCT computational thinking conceptual development scores, finding that QCT did not significantly differ across these independent variables (all reported p-values > .05 in Table 5). This indicates that teacher CT conceptual development (as measured here) may be relatively uniform across these background factors, suggesting that teacher education policy should focus less on demographic targeting and more on universal CT/ICT instructional guidance and support.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: Teachers’ positive views regarding ICT use in schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA between-subjects effects (Table 5): Graduation positive views F=16.613, p=0.002, eta^2=0.624. Experience positive views F=0.695, p=0.639, eta^2=0.258. Discipline positive views F=0.752, p=0.496, eta^2=0.131. Attending ICT–CT education positive views F=1.670, p=0.236, eta^2=0.334. ICT in schools positive views F=4.073, p=0.018, eta^2=0.803. Using ICT in schools positive views F=7.246, p=0.002, eta^2=0.867. Post hoc: as ICT use increased, positive views increased (M2–M10=-3.51, p=0.030).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged ICT level in schools, ICT use effectiveness, and background factors to predict teachers’ positive views regarding ICT use in schools, finding significant differences by ICT level and ICT use (e.g., ICT in schools: F=4.073, p=0.018; using ICT in schools: F=7.246, p=0.002) and that positive views increased as ICT use increased. This indicates that strengthening school ICT environments and supporting effective ICT use in classrooms may increase teachers’ positive attitudes toward ICT, which can facilitate CT integration in instruction.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: Teachers’ negative views regarding ICT use in schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA between-subjects effects (Table 5): Graduation negative views F=9.588, p=0.011, eta^2=0.489. Experience negative views F=8.536, p=0.002, eta^2=0.810. Discipline negative views F=0.674, p=0.531, eta^2=0.119. Attending ICT–CT education negative views F=1.648, p=0.240, eta^2=0.331. ICT in schools negative views F=5.695, p=0.006, eta^2=0.851. Using ICT in schools negative views F=9.139, p=0.001, eta^2=0.892. Post hoc: negative views decreased with high ICT levels (M4–M7=-2.48, p=0.014). Also, as professional experience increased, negative opinions increased (most significant among 25+ years).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged ICT level in schools, ICT use effectiveness, and teaching experience to predict teachers’ negative views regarding ICT use in schools, finding significant differences by ICT environment and ICT use (ICT in schools: F=5.695, p=0.006; using ICT in schools: F=9.139, p=0.001) and that negative views decreased when ICT levels were high. This indicates that improving ICT availability and enabling effective ICT use may reduce teachers’ negative perceptions, while additional professional development may be needed to address technology-related resistance among more experienced teachers.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: Teachers’ perceptions of collaboration for ICT use
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA between-subjects effects (Table 5): Graduation teachers’ collaboration F=1.410, p=0.263, eta^2=0.124. Experience teachers’ collaboration F=0.887, p=0.524, eta^2=0.307. Discipline teachers’ collaboration F=0.270, p=0.769, eta^2=0.051. Attending ICT–CT education teachers’ collaboration F=2.664, p=0.105, eta^2=0.444. ICT in schools teachers’ collaboration F=0.916, p=0.554, eta^2=0.478. Using ICT in schools teachers’ collaboration F=1.501, p=0.268, eta^2=0.575. Mean collaboration: M=13.65, SD=2.9.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged educational discipline, teaching experience, graduation level, and ICT level in schools to predict teachers’ perceptions of collaboration for ICT use, finding no statistically significant differences across these independent variables (all reported p-values > .05 in Table 5). This indicates that collaboration perceptions may be broadly shared across teacher subgroups, implying that policy efforts should target collaboration mechanisms (e.g., structured peer sharing and lesson co-planning) rather than expecting large subgroup differences.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: Teachers’ emphasis on teaching approaches to computational thinking
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA between-subjects effects (Table 5): Graduation teachers’ emphases F=3.376, p=0.096, eta^2=0.252. Experience teachers’ emphases F=0.273, p=0.918, eta^2=0.120. Discipline teachers’ emphases F=1.007, p=0.399, eta^2=0.168. Attending ICT–CT education teachers’ emphases F=0.590, p=0.635, eta^2=0.150. ICT in schools teachers’ emphases F=1.233, p=0.374, eta^2=0.552. Using ICT in schools teachers’ emphases F=2.150, p=0.124, eta^2=0.659. Mean emphases: M=30.46, SD=4.12.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged educational discipline, teaching experience, graduation level, and ICT use effectiveness to predict teachers’ emphasis on teaching approaches to computational thinking, finding no statistically significant differences across these independent variables (all reported p-values > .05 in Table 5). This indicates that CT teaching emphasis, as measured by the adapted scale, may not be strongly differentiated by these background characteristics, supporting the need for broadly accessible CT/ICT instructional guidance for all STEM teachers.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (adapted scales) — Turkey (teacher survey; no grade/domain)
main_findings.target_variable: Relationship between collaboration, CT emphasis, and ICT/CT integration (correlation outcomes)
top_predictors: Teachers’ perceptions of collaboration for ICT use
Teachers’ emphases on teaching approaches to computational thinking
Teachers’ positive views regarding ICT use in schools
Teachers’ negative views regarding ICT use in schools
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pearson correlations (Table 6): collaboration vs CT emphasis r=.501, p<.01. Positive views vs CT emphasis r=.489, p<.01. Positive views vs negative views r=-.63, p<.01. QCT vs CT emphasis r=.19 (ns) and QCT vs collaboration r=-.09 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire–adapted data from a Turkey teacher survey, the study leveraged teachers’ perceptions of collaboration and their CT teaching emphasis to examine relationships with ICT-related views, finding significant positive correlations between collaboration and CT emphasis (r=.501, p<.01) and between positive ICT views and CT emphasis (r=.489, p<.01). This indicates that fostering teacher collaboration and improving teachers’ positive perceptions of ICT may be key pathways for integrating computational thinking into classroom instruction, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This study used an online teacher survey in Turkey (n=121) drawing adapted scales from the ICILS 2018 Teacher Questionnaire and a translated QCT computational thinking test (17 items after removing two poorly functioning items). The analyses were descriptive and inferential (MANOVA for group differences and Pearson correlations), not machine-learning prediction; therefore, no PV handling, ML model metrics, or survey-weighted estimation are reported. Teachers’ QCT conceptual development scores (M=8.80, SD=2.9) did not significantly differ by educational discipline, teaching experience, graduation level, attending ICT–CT training, or ICT level in schools (Table 5). In contrast, teachers’ positive and negative ICT views differed significantly by ICT availability and ICT use in schools (e.g., positive views: ICT in schools F=4.073, p=0.018; negative views: using ICT in schools F=9.139, p=0.001). Correlational results showed collaboration and positive ICT views were associated with greater CT teaching emphasis (r=.501 and r=.489, p<.01), but the cross-sectional design prevents causal interpretation.
